analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates on consumer credit at 15% a year nationwide.
analysis.headline: The 15% interest rate cap never got a hearing or a vote: the Senate Banking Committee took no action after the bill was referred in May 2019, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for any lender to charge consumers an annual interest rate above 15%, including all finance charges, with fees barred from being used to dodge the cap. Lenders who charged more would forfeit all interest and borrowers could sue to get back everything they paid. The Federal Reserve could temporarily raise the cap if market rates rose and lender safety was threatened, and credit unions would be exempt. The bill was sent to the Senate Banking Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who pay credit card interest, payday loan customers, and anyone carrying high-rate consumer debt. Card issuers advertise average rates near or above 20%, and payday loans often cost the equivalent of several hundred percent a year, so a 15% ceiling would sharply cut what these borrowers pay. The bill also lets borrowers claw back illegally collected interest in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers with credit cards and payday loans

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on any extension of consumer credit at 15%, inclusive of all finance charges, or the lower state maximum where one applies [S3].
Blocks lenders from dodging the cap with fees, limiting non-finance-charge fees to the total finance charges allowed [S3].
Lets borrowers who were overcharged sue to recover the entire amount of interest, finance charges, and fees paid, within two years [S3].
Preserves stricter state usury laws rather than overriding them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, payday and installment lenders, and other high-rate consumer lenders, whose interest income is their core business. Some subprime borrowers could also lose access to credit altogether if lenders decide a 15% loan to a risky customer is not worth making, which is the trade-off supporters would have to defend.

drawbacks.text: A hard 15% cap could push borrowers with poor credit out of the legal lending market entirely, since lenders may simply refuse to lend to anyone they would otherwise have charged more, leaving some with fewer options than a costly loan [S3].
The bill acknowledges this risk of lender losses by letting the Federal Reserve temporarily raise the cap when rising rates threaten the safety and soundness of individual lenders [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to borrowers is large and direct: credit card interest averages well above the proposed cap, and payday lending rates run far higher. The real cost is that some high-risk borrowers might be denied credit altogether rather than offered affordable loans, which the bill's exemption for credit unions and the Fed's temporary escape valve only partly address. On balance it is a consumer-protection bill whose main downside is credit rationing at the margin.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in May 2019, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on May 9, 2019, joined by Sen. Whitehouse as the sole cosponsor [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S1].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-rate consumer lenders — credit card issuers and payday loan companies — are better off, because the 15% cap that would have cut their interest income never advanced. Borrowers paying above-15% rates gained nothing.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap consumer credit rates at 15% and referred it to the Banking Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the referred bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: An Independent sponsored the bill with a single Democratic cosponsor and no Republican support, and the Republican-controlled Banking Committee left it untouched.

industries.note: Their business model depends on rates far above 15%; the cap would effectively shut down most of their lending, and the fees they charge borrowers would be capped too.
Typical card rates exceed the proposed cap, so interest income on revolving balances — a major profit center — would be cut sharply, with lenders liable to refund illegally collected interest.
The bill explicitly exempts insured credit unions from the rate cap, letting them serve borrowers at rates competitors could no longer charge.
